title: Shloka 50
subtitle: The end of the negations, and Durgā

namas.translation: No balance can weigh her, because there is nothing to put in the other pan.

compound.gloss: she for whom there is no counterweight

children.gloss: a balance or scale, and so equality and comparison

namas.translation: The hair of her head is a deep blue-black, falling dark across all that brightness.

morphology.note: The first member is nīla, 'dark', not the privative nis- that opens the names around it.

namas.translation: Nothing departs from her and nothing in her wears out.

compound.gloss: she in whom there is no wasting away

namas.translation: No lapse and no peril touches her, and time finds nothing in her to spend.

compound.gloss: she for whom there is no passing away or peril

children.gloss: passing away, and so danger or transgression

namas.translation: She is not easily got hold of, and the difficulty is part of what she is rather than an obstacle in front of her.

children.gloss: the obtaining, the getting of a thing

namas.translation: The way to her is rough going, and not many walk it to the end.

children.gloss: going, the traversing of a way

namas.translation: She is the stronghold no one can storm, and under this name she is the warrior goddess herself.

morphology.note: Grammatically dus + √gam, 'hard of access'; the tradition also derives the name from an Asura called Durga whom she is said to have killed.

namas.translation: She strikes pain down rather than merely consoling the one who is in it.

children.gloss: a slayer, one who strikes down

namas.translation: Having taken the pain away she does not leave the space empty but fills it with ease.

commentary.meaning: The long negative run finishes in the first line of this verse and then the hymn changes prefix. Four last removals — nothing to weigh her against, nothing that departs from her, nothing that lapses — and among them, without warning, her hair. Nīlacikurā is a plain physical description dropped into the middle of metaphysics, the same intrusion that put her face and her waist into the verse where the negations began, and it is the one dark thing in a goddess who has been red since the meditation verses. Then dur- takes over from nir- and the grammar is identical while the sense is opposite: hard to obtain, hard to approach, and then, in two syllables, Durgā — the only place in the thousand names where that name appears. The verse closes with the first straightforwardly positive pair in fifty-six names. She strikes sorrow down, and having taken it away she does not leave the space empty.
commentary.history:
The negative series ends at niratyayā, the hundred and eighty-seventh name, having run without a break since nirādhārā. What follows is not a change of method but a change of material. The prefix dus behaves exactly as nis does: it becomes dur before a vowel or a voiced consonant, and it keeps a visarga before the unvoiced kh of duḥkha, which is precisely the pattern the reciter has spent seven verses learning. What has changed is the meaning. Nis subtracts; dus says that a thing is hard or bad. The hymn hands the same machine to a different word and produces the opposite kind of epithet, and the seam is at the end of the first line.

Nistulā is the best of the last four. Tulā is a balance, the pair of scales, and it is also the word for the ordeal by weighing in the law books, in which an accused person is placed in one pan and matched against a counterweight. From that comes the whole vocabulary of comparison: to be equal to something is to be in the balance with it. The stotra has spent forty verses comparing her to things, and much of the classical poetry that stands behind it — the Saundaryalaharī's weighing of her lips against coral and the bimba fruit, for instance — is built on the figure of the failed comparison. Nistulā says that there is nothing to put in the other pan.

Then the hair. This is the third time a body has broken into an abstract passage in this batch, after the autumn-moon face and the slender waist seven verses back, and it is the most conspicuous because of the colour. Nīla is the blue-black of the rain cloud and of the blue lotus, and in a hymn where she has been red from the first meditation verse — vermilion, dawn-coloured, a flood of red light drowning the world-eggs — her hair is the single dark thing about her. The Saundaryalaharī compares that mass of hair to a grove of blue lotuses and then claims that heaven's flowers move into it for the sake of its natural scent, which is the fullest treatment the tradition gives the image.

Durgā is the event of this verse. Of the thousand names, this is the only one that is simply the name of another goddess in her own right and nothing more, and it goes past in two syllables. Its oldest sense is not a person at all. In the Veda durga is a hard place: a defile, a difficult crossing, a stronghold. The hymn of the Durgā Sūkta asks Agni to carry us over all difficult places as a boat carries one over a river, and the Kaṭha Upaniṣad calls the path to the self a razor's edge, hard to cross, and says that the wise call that path a durga. Both of those senses sit inside the names on either side. Durlabhā, hard to get, and durgamā, hard to approach, are not describing an obstacle standing in front of her; they are saying that the difficulty is what she is. And durga as fortress gives the name its other classical reading, the stronghold that cannot be stormed.

What the name also does is import a whole other goddess and her literature. Durgā of the Devī Māhātmya is the warrior who kills Mahiṣa and Śumbha, and the great hymns of that text are addressed to her by name; one of the best known asks who but she, remembered, takes away the fear of every living creature, and calls her the remover of poverty, sorrow and fear. Two of those three appear here. Duḥkhahantrī is the next name but one, and bhayāpahā was a name eight verses back. The Lalitā tradition and the Devī Māhātmya tradition are distinct — different texts, different rites, different lineages — and this is one of the places where the later hymn reaches over and takes what it needs.

Duḥkhahantrī and sukhapradā close the verse and turn the hymn round. For fifty-six names the method has been removal; the last pair removes something and then puts something in its place. It is the hinge into the verses that follow, where every name will begin with sarva, all.
commentary.practice:
Two prefixes, one grammar. In the first line nis appears as nis before the dental t of nistulā, as nī with a long vowel and no consonant before the r of nīrāgā's cousin — here nī-la, though that nī is part of the word for blue and not the prefix at all, which is exactly the trap — and as nir before the vowels of nirapāyā and niratyayā. In the second line dus appears as dur before the voiced l and g of durlabhā, durgamā and durgā, and as duḥ before the unvoiced kh of duḥkhahantrī. Learning that these are two words behaving identically, rather than four or five separate forms, is the single most useful thing this verse teaches.

Nīlacikurā is where reciters go wrong, because after seven verses of ni- prefixes the ear expects another one. It is not. The word is nīla, blue-black, with a long ī, and then cikura, hair. Four short syllables follow the long one: nī-la-ci-ku-rā. Get the length of that first syllable right and the metre holds; treat it as a negative prefix and the whole quarter collapses.

Duḥkha has to be given its visarga. It is duḥ, with a light voiceless breath echoing the u, and then kha, an aspirated guttural. It is not dukkha, which is the Pali form and which most English speakers have met first, and it is not duka. The h of the visarga and the h of the aspiration are two separate events. Say duḥ-kha-han-trī slowly; there are three h sounds in the word and each is doing a different job.

The cluster ntr in hantrī is the same one that appeared in mamatāhantrī three verses ago, and the same feminine agent ending. Sukhapradā, by contrast, is four completely open syllables and is the easiest word in the batch — which is appropriate, since it is the only name in fifty-six that gives something outright.

Durgā is two syllables and both are heavy: dur with a full r, gā long. It is the shortest name in this batch and it should not be hurried through on the way to the next one. In practice many reciters mark it, slightly, and there is a reason to.

The metre is worth noticing because the third quarter repeats a rhythm from earlier in the batch exactly. Durlabhā durgamā durgā is three plus three plus two, which is the shape of nirlepā nirmalā nityā six verses back. The first quarter is three plus five, the second and fourth are four plus four. Breathe after niratyayā, which is also where the negations stop.

For contemplation this verse offers a change of posture. Fifty-six names have been removals, and it is possible to chant them and end up somewhere rather cold. The last two names of this verse are the tradition's own correction. Sorrow is struck down, which is a violent word, and then something is handed over. The traditional use of the verse follows the same logic: this is the passage people recite for someone who is suffering, and the name they are reciting toward is the last one.

crossReferences.deva: उत्तिष्ठत जाग्रत प्राप्य वरान्निबोधत । क्षुरस्य धारा निशिता दुरत्यया दुर्गं पथस्तत्कवयो वदन्ति ॥
crossReferences.iast: uttiṣṭhata jāgrata prāpya varān nibodhata | kṣurasya dhārā niśitā duratyayā durgaṃ pathas tat kavayo vadanti ||
crossReferences.translation: Get up. Wake. Go to those who can give you what you need, and understand. Sharp as a razor's edge and hard to cross — the poets say that this path is a durga.
crossReferences.relevance: Three of the words in this verse of the stotra, in one line of an upaniṣad: durga, duratyayā, and the idea behind durgamā and durlabhā. Note that the Kaṭha applies the word to the path and not to a person. When the stotra makes durgā a name, the difficulty of the road and the identity of the goal have been folded together, which is exactly what durlabhā, hard to obtain, is saying about her.

crossReferences.deva: जातवेदसे सुनवाम सोममरातीयतो निदहाति वेदः । स नः पर्षदति दुर्गाणि विश्वा नावेव सिन्धुं दुरितात्यग्निः ॥
crossReferences.iast: jātavedase sunavāma somam arātīyato nidahāti vedaḥ | sa naḥ parṣad ati durgāṇi viśvā nāveva sindhuṃ duritāty agniḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: For Jātavedas let us press the soma; may he burn up the possessions of the man who is hostile to us. May he carry us across every hard place, as a boat across a river — Agni, across all difficulty.
crossReferences.relevance: The Vedic verse from which the tradition derives the name Durgā, and the oldest evidence for what the word originally meant. Durgāṇi here is a plural noun for hard passages in the landscape, not a divine name, and the prayer is to be ferried over them. Every later reading of Durgā as the stronghold, or as the one who is hard to reach, or as the one who takes you across, is contained in this one line.

crossReferences.deva: दुर्गे स्मृता हरसि भीतिमशेषजन्तोः स्वस्थैः स्मृता मतिमतीव शुभां ददासि । दारिद्र्यदुःखभयहारिणि का त्वदन्या सर्वोपकारकरणाय सदार्द्रचित्ता ॥
crossReferences.iast: durge smṛtā harasi bhītim aśeṣajantoḥ svasthaiḥ smṛtā matim atīva śubhāṃ dadāsi | dāridryaduḥkhabhayahāriṇi kā tvad anyā sarvopakārakaraṇāya sadārdracittā ||
crossReferences.translation: Durgā — remembered, you take away the fear of every creature there is; remembered by those who are already well, you give them a mind of extraordinary goodness. Taker-away of poverty, sorrow and fear, who is there but you, whose heart is always wet for the doing of good to all?
crossReferences.relevance: The name Durgā as the other great goddess text uses it, and the source of much of what this verse assumes. Three things are removed there — poverty, sorrow and fear — and two of them are names in this batch, duḥkhahantrī here and bhayāpahā eight verses back. The last line is also the best gloss available on sāndrakaruṇā in the next verse: a heart that is permanently wet.

crossReferences.deva: धुनोतु ध्वान्तं नस्तुलितदलितेन्दीवरवनं घनस्निग्धश्लक्ष्णं चिकुरनिकुरुम्बं तव शिवे । यदीयं सौरभ्यं सहजमुपलब्धुं सुमनसो वसन्त्यस्मिन्मन्ये वलमथनवाटीविटपिनाम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: dhunotu dhvāntaṃ nas tulitadalitendīvaravanaṃ ghanasnigdhaślakṣṇaṃ cikuranikurumbaṃ tava śive | yadīyaṃ saurabhyaṃ sahajam upalabdhuṃ sumanaso vasanty asmin manye valamathanavāṭīviṭapinām ||
crossReferences.translation: May the great mass of your hair shake off our darkness, Śivā — thick, glossy and smooth, a match for a grove of blue lotuses in flower. I think the blossoms of Indra's garden trees have gone to live in it in order to acquire its natural fragrance.
crossReferences.relevance: The same word, cikura, and the same colour. Śaṅkara's verse supplies what the sahasranāma's single compound leaves out: why a poet would bother to say that a goddess has dark hair. Blue-black is the colour of the indīvara lotus and of the rain cloud, and in a figure this old the darkness of the hair is set to work against the darkness it is asked to disperse.

references.note: The hymn quoted above is in the fourth chapter, sung by the gods after the killing of Mahiṣa. Read it alongside the eleventh chapter's Nārāyaṇī stuti, and the whole vocabulary the sahasranāma borrows for Durgā is in front of you in two pages.

references.note: A translation with a long essay on how the text has actually been used. The relevant question for this verse is what it means for a later hymn to borrow one name from an earlier cult, and Coburn is the best guide to what is being borrowed.
